description: This topic covers various types of computer networks such as Local Area Network (LAN) and Wide Area Network (WAN). It also provides a detailed explanation of network topologies, which refers to the physical or logical arrangement of nodes in a network.

sections.title: Types of Computer Networks
sections.description: Classification of computer networks based on their geographical coverage area and size.

key_concepts.explanation: Connects devices within an individual's personal workspace. Its typical range is about 10 meters. Bluetooth and USB are common examples.
Connects computers and devices within a small geographical area such as a home, school, or single building. Ethernet and Wi-Fi are primary examples.
Covers an entire city or a large educational/corporate campus. It is larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN. Cable TV networks are a prime example.
Spans a very large geographical area, such as a country or continent. It typically utilizes telecommunication lines or satellite links.

key_associations.extra_info: Used for highly secure, short-distance wireless or wired communication.
It is the largest WAN in existence, universally known as the 'network of networks'.

sections.title: Basics of Network Topology
sections.description: Fundamental terminology defining the structural layout of devices in a computer network.

key_concepts.explanation: The physical or logical geometric arrangement in which various nodes or computers are connected to each other in a network.
Any physical device connected to a network, such as a computer, printer, or router, that is capable of generating, receiving, or forwarding data.

sections.title: Major Network Topologies - Part 1
sections.description: The simplest and most commonly utilized basic network structures.

key_concepts.explanation: All nodes are connected sequentially to a single main cable, known as the backbone. If the main backbone cable fails, the entire network goes down.
All nodes are independently connected to a central networking device, such as a Hub or a Switch. The network fails entirely only if this central device fails.
Each node is connected to exactly two other neighboring nodes, forming a closed loop or circular path. Data generally flows in a single, unidirectional path.

sections.title: Complex Network Topologies - Part 2
sections.description: Advanced network structures typically deployed for larger and more secure enterprise networks.

key_concepts.explanation: Every node is directly connected to every other node in the network via dedicated point-to-point links. It is the most reliable and secure topology but requires extensive cabling and cost.
A combination of characteristics from both bus and star topologies, creating a hierarchical, root-and-branch structure. It is also referred to as hierarchical topology.
A custom combination of two or more different types of standard topologies, such as connecting a local Star network to a broader Ring network.

sections.title: Important Facts
sections.description: Crucial, exam-oriented one-liner facts related to network architectures and topologies.

important_facts.fact: Star Topology is currently the most widely deployed topology in modern networks because it is the easiest to install, manage, and troubleshoot.
In a fully connected Mesh Topology, to connect 'n' number of nodes to each other, exactly n(n-1)/2 physical channels (cables) are required.
Ring Topology utilizes a specialized control mechanism called 'Token Passing' to authorize data transmission and prevent data packet collisions.
In a Bus Topology, devices called 'Terminators' are placed at both extreme ends of the backbone cable to absorb signals and prevent them from bouncing back.
